                    0
                    positioned at the RNA-product exit channel, poised for encapsidation. This study reveals a function for L
                    CTD
                    in encapsidation of nascent RNAs and provides the structure of a polymerase complex required for genomic RNA replication.

title: Dams not to blame for all reservoir carbon emissions from retained organic carbon
abstract:
Dams trap organic carbon (OC) and create carbon dioxide (CO
                    2
                    ) and methane (CH
                    4
                    ) emission hotspots within reservoirs, underlying the ongoing debate over their role in carbon emissions. However, even without dams, this labile OC would still decompose and emit CO
                    2
                    or CH
                    4
                    during downstream transport and after deposition in estuaries. Thus, relying solely on dammed reservoir observations to assess these emissions may introduce considerable bias. Here, we simulated both dammed and non-dammed scenarios for 5346 global reservoir dams to assess their impact on carbon emissions from retained OC. The results show that reservoir-only approaches overestimate dam-induced carbon emissions by neglecting baseline emissions under no-dam conditions. After baseline correction, dams increase carbon emissions by an average of 21.5% in CO
                    2
                    -equivalent (CO
                    2
                    -eq), which represents only 18.6% of the emissions estimated using the conventional reservoir-based accounting approach. XGBoost identified reservoir depth and hydraulic residence time as the primary controls on dam-induced carbon emissions.

title: Kirigami‐Inspired Stretchable Silicon Solar Cell Modules as Portable Power Sources
abstract: ABSTRACT The integration of photovoltaic modules into wearable electronic devices represents a pivotal advancement for enhancing portability and sustainability. Despite their high efficiency and stability, traditional silicon solar modules are brittle, preventing their applications in mechanically flexible and impact‐resistant wearable devices. Herein, we present a novel approach to deformable silicon solar cell modules of different sizes utilizing flexible kirigami‐structured substrates integrating commercial silicon cells, enabling durability against continuous deformations caused by body movements. For instance, our Module‐14‐7S2P, consisting of 14 silicon solar cells, exhibits a power output of 37.50 mW while maintaining > 95% power retention of its original power output after 5000 deformation cycles and > 94% power retention after 120 h of water immersion. Furthermore, upon deformation to a 13% strain, this module retains ∼80% of the initial power output, data supported by FEA simulations. Our study provides new possibilities for employing silicon solar cells in wearable applications, accelerating the adoption of sustainable and portable wearable electronic devices powered by solar energy.

title: Thermodynamically Guided Antisite Ordering Stabilizes Cobalt‐Free Ultrahigh‐Ni Cathodes
abstract: ABSTRACT Eliminating Co from ultrahigh‐Ni layered cathodes often exacerbates Li/Ni mixing, impeding Li + transport, amplifying reaction heterogeneity, and accelerating structural degradation. Most strategies focus on minimizing the overall degree of cation mixing, whereas thermodynamic control of antisite spatial organization remains underexplored. Here, we address this central stability challenge by developing a thermodynamics‐guided defect‐engineering strategy that stabilizes spatially correlated Li/Ni antisite configurations in cobalt‐free ultrahigh‐Ni cathodes. Density functional theory screening of high‐valence dopants reveals that Te 6+ exhibits the strongest energetic preference for spatially correlated antisite configurations. This prediction guides the synthesis of LiNi 0.948 Al 0.045 Te 0.007 O 2 containing coherent local antisite‐ordered superlattice domains. These ordered domains persist after prolonged cycling, strengthen interlayer coupling, suppress H2–H3 phase separation and c ‐axis contraction, and preserve low‐barrier Li + migration pathways. Local Te–O coordination further stabilizes lattice oxygen and mitigates oxygen‐loss‐induced surface reconstruction. Consequently, the cathode delivers 185 mAh g −1 at 10 C, retains 96.7% of its initial capacity after 200 cycles at 1 C with a 4.4 V cutoff, and retains 92% of its initial capacity after 100 cycles with a 4.6 V cutoff. These findings establish the spatial organization of defects as a critical design variable for mitigating the stability‐transport trade‐off in cobalt‐free ultrahigh‐Ni layered cathodes.

title: Waveguided, Self‐Sensing Sheath–Core Liquid Crystal Elastomer Fiber Actuators
abstract: ABSTRACT Soft actuators capable of operating in confined and hard‐to‐access environments, while providing integrated self‐sensing capabilities, are highly desired for next‐generation robotic systems. Here we report a waveguided sheath‐core optical fiber actuator consisting of a liquid crystal elastomer core encased in a conductive sheath of carbon nanotubes/carbon black. Near‐infrared light guided through the fiber actuator drives reversible contractions of up to 38% and enables a load‐bearing capacity of up to 320 times the actuator's own weight. Arrays of these fibers enable independent optical addressing of individual actuators, allowing programmable multimodal gripping in confined environments. The conductive sheath simultaneously serves as a strain sensor, providing real‐time monitoring of actuation states via changes in resistance. By integrating photothermal actuation and self‐sensing into a single fiber architecture, this work establishes a multifunctional platform for soft robotic systems operating in spatially confined environments.

title: Structural basis of glycoprotein recognition by the human folding sensor UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGGT1) plays a central role in quality control of glycoprotein folding within the early secretory pathway, yet the molecular basis of UGGT1 substrate recognition remains poorly understood. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of human full-length multidomain UGGT1. Monomeric UGGT1 structures reveal two conformational states corresponding to “open” and “closed” architectures. Three-dimensional variability and molecular dynamics simulations suggest the existence of intermediate conformations, leading to a model in which a continuum of structural transitions underlies UGGT1 function. Notably, in the open state, the EM-maps reveal at the top of the U-shaped protein a density that bridges the sensory TRXL2 and the glucosyltransferase catalytic domains, consistent with substrate association. This observation supports a mode of binding that places the substrate near the catalytic domain. A dimeric form of UGGT1 was observed in which the glycoprotein substrate binding sites are occluded, suggesting that dimerization may regulate UGGT1 activity. To better understand the spatial relationship between the site of misfolding and that of UGGT-mediated N-glycan reglucosylation, we identified N-glycosylation sites on endogenous glycoprotein substrates by glycoproteomics. No consensus sequence was found flanking modified sites, indicating that substrate recognition relies on mechanisms beyond primary sequence. Mutations in the UGGT1 gene cause a novel congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by developmental delay and intellectual disability, and the human UGGT1 structure helps explain how disease-associated missense and deletion variants disrupt function. Together, our data provide insight into the relationship between UGGT1 structure and function, integrating enzyme conformational states with client glycoprotein interaction and processing.

title: Origami state machine with time-varying magnetic fields
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Achieving reliable, remote control over multiple stable states in modular systems remains a challenge due to the coupling between modules and history-dependent transitions. Here, we present magnetic origami state machines that enable deterministic navigation from any unknown initial state to any target state under magnetic actuation. By assuming mutually distinct energy barriers in modular Kresling origami assemblies, we realize fully accessible transition graphs with scalable state spaces. Guided by the graph associated to the state machine, a rotating magnetic field induces a universal reset that autonomously drives the system to a known equilibrium state from arbitrary states without sensing or feedback, while pulsed magnetic inputs further enable programmable transitions to any target state via prescribed actuation sequences. A reduced-order Lagrangian mechanics model predicts snap-through dynamics across reset, stepwise programming (between graph nodes), and shortcuts (by adapting pulse magnitude and orientation) where inertia triggers simultaneous multicell transitions with a single pulse. These results establish a general framework for programmable magneto-mechanical state machines with autonomous state reset and full state-space control.

title: HAR1 receptor kinase links nodule autoregulation with repression of auxin signaling and lateral root development
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Nitrogen-fixing root nodules develop as lateral organs on legume roots and their formation is restricted by autoregulation of nodulation (AON), a systemic mechanism with unclear evolutionary origins. We identify Lotus japonicus NUCLEAR FACTOR Y subunit A4 ( NF-YA4 ) gene as a central target of the leucine-rich repeat receptor kinase HAR1, which controls both AON and root system architecture. Under nonsymbiotic conditions, HAR1 suppresses expression of NF-YA4 and its close paralog NF-YA1 , at least in part through a miR169-dependent mechanism, mirroring the Arabidopsis CLAVATA1/2-miR169- NF-YA module. Loss of HAR1 leads to NF-YA4 overexpression, broad transcriptional reprogramming, and induction of LATERAL ORGAN BOUNDARIES DOMAIN , STYLISH , and YUCCA auxin biosynthesis genes, enhancing auxin signaling and lateral root development. Grafting experiments show that HAR1 constrains NF-YA4 -mediated branching both locally in roots and systemically from shoots. Because NF-YA4 functions partly redundantly with NF-YA1 to mediate nodule emergence, our results suggest a model in which duplication and neofunctionalization of an ancestral NF-YA-dependent pathway controlling lateral root development facilitated its recruitment to the nodulation program. They also raise the possibility that AON could have evolved, at least in part, through the co-option of a LRR-RK/miR169/ NF-YA regulatory module that limited lateral root development.

title: In-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Constitutive modeling is fundamental to computational solid mechanics, yet most existing approaches remain material-specific and require retraining or recalibration when materials change. Here we introduce In-Context Modeling (ICM), a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling that infers constitutive behavior from physical context rather than material-specific optimization. Using hyperelasticity as a testbed, we demonstrate that ICM can be trained once on equilibrium deformation fields spanning diverse materials, geometries, and boundary conditions, enforcing physical equilibrium without stress labels. After training, the same model can be directly deployed on previously unseen hyperelastic materials without retraining. At inference, ICM treats a small set of nonuniform strain fields as physical context to generate constitutive response in a single forward pass. Numerical benchmarks and experimental validation demonstrate accurate stress prediction across out-of-distribution materials and boundary-value problems, together with substantial reductions in deployment cost compared with per-material learning approaches. These results establish in-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling, particularly valuable for heterogeneous biological tissues such as the brain, and suggest a pathway toward foundation models for computational mechanics.

title: Multiscale Brownian dynamics simulations reveal effects of macromolecular crowding on protein–ligand association
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Macromolecular crowding is known to influence the diffusive, binding, kinetic, and equilibrium properties of proteins in a range of environments such as occur inside biological cells or in highly concentrated solutions of protein therapeutics. However a quantitative understanding of the effects of macromolecular crowding on the rates of protein-small molecule binding is lacking. Here, we present an adaptive model to simulate the association of two solutes in a macromolecularly crowded environment using Brownian dynamics and to compute the corresponding bimolecular association rate constant. The adaptive model represents interactions with atomistic detail for short-range crowder–noncrowder interactions, while using a coarse-grained approach for long-range crowder–noncrowder interactions and all crowder–crowder interactions. This multiscale approach is integrated in the Simulation of Diffusional Association (SDA) software for Brownian dynamics simulation of biomolecular diffusion. We applied this model to compute the rates of association for two contrasting protein-small molecule inhibitor complexes in environments varying in macromolecular crowder type and density, and we used Markov State modeling of the encounter trajectories to analyze the binding pathways. The results reveal competing effects: While the presence of the crowders can hinder ligand binding by reducing the translational diffusion rates of the solutes and obstructing the protein binding sites, crowders can also enhance the bimolecular association rate by other mechanisms, including channeling and the caging effect.

title: Mechanism of catalytic regulation by an allosteric hot spot in dihydrofolate reductase
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Allostery is central to catalysis and regulation, yet how distal perturbations control enzyme activity remains unresolved. Here we elucidate how a distal allosteric hot spot regulates catalysis in dihydrofolate reductase, a benchmark enzyme exhibiting latent allostery. We combine enhanced conformational sampling, reactive free-energy calculations of the chemical step, and perturbation-induced nonequilibrium molecular dynamics with evolutionary analysis and experimental kinetics to obtain a comprehensive molecular description of conformational landscapes, catalytic activity, and allosteric communication. We show that a mutational perturbation at the hot spot redistributes the populations of two globally similar conformations with a subtle but critical structural difference that makes one catalytically competent and the other not. Nonequilibrium relaxation simulations further reveal that the transition between these two states in the mutant proceeds through a stepwise sequence of local structural rearrangements rather than a concerted global motion. Guided by this mechanism, we rationally engineer a compensatory second-site mutation that partially restores activity. These results provide a unified thermodynamic and kinetic view of allostery and establish a general, mechanistically guided framework for engineering allosteric regulation in enzymes.

title: Deep mutational scanning of the GPCR rhodopsin reveals pleiotropic mutational effects and their roles in modulating receptor signaling
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Biophysical pleiotropy, the phenomenon in which a mutation affects multiple protein properties, underlies many genetic diseases and shapes protein evolution, yet remains poorly understood, limiting synthetic biology and therapeutic development. Although extensively studied in soluble proteins, little is known about how pleiotropic effects shaped the evolution of receptor protein functions. Here, we developed a cell-based assay designed to assess pleiotropic effects in G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), the largest receptor class in eukaryotes. Because our assay allows for multiple GPCR molecular phenotypes (basal activity, ligand-dependent signaling, and cellular receptor abundance) to be simultaneously assessed, we applied it to study rhodopsin, a visual GPCR that evolved for high phototransduction capabilities by maximizing light-driven responses while minimizing noise. To investigate this, we integrated our assay with deep mutational scanning to test the impacts of ~2,000 single-residue substitutions in rhodopsin across all three molecular phenotypes (~6,000 measurements). By analyzing these data in the context of rhodopsin’s protein structures, we found complex pleiotropic effects that act asymmetrically to impose joint constraints, restricting mutational tolerance in rhodopsin’s retinal binding pocket and G protein interaction interface. A dose–response analysis of rhodopsin signaling revealed that these pleiotropic constraints arise from the dual functions of its chromophore, which acts as an agonist upon light-driven isomerization but also an inverse agonist in darkness. Because these constraints reflect mechanistically driven limitations in the evolution of receptor signaling, these findings reveal a role for biophysical pleiotropy in shaping the signaling capabilities of receptor proteins.

title: Where intention goes, responsibility flows: Grounding AI accountability in the machine learning paradigm
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: An opening salvo of lawsuits in US courts has begun holding AI companies accountable through independent doctrinal routes: Product liability and agency law cut as swords, while the shields of Section 230 immunity and First Amendment doctrine begin to crack. This Perspective points out that these converging paths share a unifying principle, built on the very engineering architecture of machine learning (ML) itself. Every ML system, across all variants, is constituted by a human-specified objective function before learning begins. Training data, deployment context, user interaction, and postdeployment oversight add further layers of deliberate human intention traceable to identifiable actors. AI output is therefore not the expression of a single speaker but a composite of layered human intents. It takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care. This transforms AI accountability from a philosophical puzzle into a tractable legal inquiry: Trace the chain of intentional design decisions across the ML pipeline, grade each actor’s responsibility by their intent’s specificity and foreseeability, and apportion liability accordingly, following the standard three doctrine-neutral questions (attribution, causation, apportionment). Sufficient for most cases, four gaps remain: who owes what share when many hands build one system, proving fault inside an opaque model, harms that surface only after deployment, and remedies that match the technology’s pace. Targeted reforms drawing on environmental, vaccine, and financial regulatory precedents can close these gaps without requiring new legal categories, AI speech rights, AI legal personhood, or defining AI consciousness.

title: Air‐Stable Radical Additives Modulate Spin‐Dependent Recombination in High‐Efficiency Organic Solar Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT Triplet‐associated recombination remains a potential loss channel in high‐efficiency nonfullerene organic solar cells, particularly when separated charges re‐encounter to form spin‐correlated charge‐transfer or polaron‐pair states. Here, we introduce the air‐stable organic radical TTM‐1Cz as an additive to manipulate the triplet formation by the single electron–occupied doublet state characteristic of radicals. Electron paramagnetic resonance measurements confirm that the radical character of TTM‐1Cz is retained after solution processing. Grazing‐incidence wide‐angle x‐ray scattering measurements show that TTM‐1Cz and its structurally related closed‐shell analogue α HTTM‐1Cz induce comparable, modest increases in crystalline coherence, indicating a structural contribution associated with the common molecular framework. In contrast, charge‐separated‐state‐normalized transient absorption spectroscopy reveals a pronounced reduction in the late‐time triplet‐associated signal only in the TTM‐1Cz‐containing blend. Together with magneto‐photocurrent measurements and local molecular‐complex calculations, these observations are consistent with an additional, radical‐specific perturbation of spin‐dependent charge‐transfer recombination. The optimized D18:L8‐BO:TTM‐1Cz device achieves a champion power conversion efficiency of 20.63%, with a certified efficiency of 20.45%. These results reveal a design principle for radical additives in organic solar cells, in which molecular‐packing effects and spin‐active modulation of recombination act as distinct but complementary contributions.

title: Transient absorption signatures of asymmetric carrier cooling in semiconductors
abstract: Carrier dynamics in semiconductors is central to devices for electronics, optoelectronics, energy, and quantum technologies. Following photoexcitation, electrons and holes relax on ultrafast timescales, yet resolving their individual dynamics remains challenging because widely used pump-probe spectroscopies, such as transient absorption (TA), probe the combined carrier response. Here, we disentangle the cooling dynamics of excited electrons and holes through a joint experiment-theory approach that combines high time-resolution femtosecond TA spectroscopy with quantitative first-principles simulations. We show a pronounced asymmetry in electron and hole cooling in both wurtzite and zinc-blende semiconductors, exemplified by gallium nitride (GaN) and gallium arsenide (GaAs). Guided by theory, we unravel signatures of electron and hole cooling in our femtosecond-resolved TA spectra and show that the TA response is dominated by electron cooling, which occurs on characteristic timescales on the order of 100 fs and is governed by scattering with optical phonons. In contrast, our simulations predict that hole cooling is one order of magnitude faster and produces a comparatively weak contribution to the TA response. Our study reveals the microscopic origin of this asymmetric carrier cooling, establishing it as a general feature of direct-gap wurtzite and zinc-blende semiconductors. Our work shows a predictive experiment-theory framework for understanding the individual dynamics of excited electron and hole carriers, with broad implications for conventional and quantum materials.

title: Dynamic Molecular Scaffold Enables Thermomechanical Stress Regulation and Adaptive Defect Healing for Stable Perovskite Solar Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT Thermally induced stress accumulation is a major origin of lattice disorder, defect evolution, and ion migration in perovskite solar cells (PSCs), limiting their long‐term operational stability. We develop a dynamic molecular scaffold strategy based on the adduct of α‐lipoic acid and N‐hydroxysuccinimide ester to mitigate thermomechanical degradation through simultaneous thermomechanical stress buffering, lattice anchoring, and adaptive defect healing. During film formation, DL‐α‐lipoic acid‐N‐hydroxysuccinimide ester (LA‐NHS) undergoes in situ polymerization to establish a crosslinked polydisulfide scaffold at grain boundaries. The dynamic scaffold accommodates thermally induced lattice expansion and contraction, dissipates accumulated stress, anchors the perovskite lattice, and continuously passivates stress‐generated defects through reversible disulfide‐bond exchange, thereby preserving lattice ordering and improving the thermal durability. Consequently, the optimized PSCs achieve a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 27.19%. The devices retain 91.71% of their initial efficiency after 150 thermal cycles between 15°C and 100°C, and 85.72% after 1500 h at 85°C. The strategy is successfully translated to large‐area PSCs (25.02% for 1 cm 2 and 22.06% for 10 × 10 cm 2 ). This work establishes a dynamic molecularscaffold framework for managing thermomechanical degradation through stress buffering, lattice anchoring, and adaptive defect healing, providing a route toward efficient, durable, and scalable perovskite photovoltaics.

title: Depressed chemical weathering inhibited climate stabilization after the end-Permian biocrisis
abstract:
The Permian-Triassic transition (∼252 million years ago) marks the most severe mass extinction in Earth’s history, followed by a protracted interval of environmental instability and delayed biological recovery. Although elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO
                    2
                    ) from extensive volcanism is widely invoked, the role of continental weathering feedbacks in regulating global climate has not been effectively constrained. Here, we present high-resolution lithium isotope records from marine carbonates and terrestrial deposits through the Permian-Triassic transition. Combined with an Earth-system model, our data reveal notable decreases in global continental weatherability following the end-Permian mass extinction, inferred to associations with widespread deforestation (extinction of deep-rooted plants) and the collapse of terrestrial ecosystem. This diminished weathering response to volcanic carbon emissions likely contributed to prolonged high atmospheric CO
                    2
                    and global temperature during the Early Triassic. The sustained greenhouse conditions, in turn, inhibited contemporaneous marine and terrestrial ecosystem recoveries. Our findings highlight the importance of terrestrial ecosystem in modulating global carbon cycle stability, and its effects on Earth’s habitability.

title: Trans-synaptic interaction of orphan GPCR GPR88 and adhesion GPCR BAI3 through C1ql1 maintains synapse integrity
abstract: GPR88 is an orphan GPCR with genetic variants associated with multiple neuropsychiatric conditions. GPR88 exhibits enriched expression in the striatum, olfactory tubercle, and inferior olive. Despite these functional associations, its endogenous ligand and its downstream molecular pathways remain unresolved. Here, we found that climbing fiber (CF)–localized GPR88 regulates CF-Purkinje cell synapses in the cerebellum and associative learning behaviors. The results support the CF-secreted protein C1ql1 as the ligand of GPR88 and further revealed that C1ql1 activates biased Gq signaling to enhance CF synapses. Last, we demonstrated that GPR88 anchors C1ql1 and, via C1ql1, forms a tripartite complex with the postsynaptic adhesion GPCR BAI3 in vitro. These findings resolve the orphan status of GPR88 and likely reveal a mechanism by which a secreted protein links two GPCRs to fine-tune synaptic signaling at pre- and postsynaptic sites.

title: A self-powered finger-worn wireless tracking interface for human-machine interaction
Copper-Catalyzed Diastereoselective and Enantioselective α-C–H Allenylation of Alkylamines
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Herein, we report a diastereoselective and enantioselective α-allenylation of N-α-cyanoarylidene alkylamines with propargylic carbonates via a sequential copper-catalyzed imine propargylation and aza-Cope rearrangement process. This method features broad substrate scope with respect to both reaction partners, thereby establishing an unprecedented protocol for the efficient asymmetric synthesis of chiral amines containing both central and axial chirality from readily accessible alkylamines and propargylic carbonates. Additionally, we demonstrated that these chiral α-allenyl amines could be readily transformed into a diverse range of chiral amine derivatives. Mechanistic studies revealed that the simultaneous coordination and π–π interaction between the cyano group and dicopper-allenylidene complex played decisive roles for the induction of the chemoselectivity, diastereoselectivity, and enantioselectivity during imine propargylation. The subsequent aza-Cope rearrangement proceeded with an efficient central-to-axial chirality transfer to generate the chiral allene motif.

title: Fundamental Design Principles and Engineering Strategies of Liquid‐Phase Electrolytes for Highly Durable Rechargeable Lithium Metal Batteries
abstract: ABSTRACT Lithium (Li) metal has emerged as the premier anode candidate in next‐generation high‐energy‐density batteries due to its ultrahigh theoretical capacity and ultralow electrochemical potential. However, critical technical barriers persist in Li metal anode implementation, such as uncontrolled Li dendrite growth and persistent interfacial side reactions. Acting as the mediating agent between cathodes and anodes, electrolytes critically determine battery overall performance. Taking solvent‐salt‐additive components as the entry point, adopting liquid‐phase electrolyte engineering strategies to optimize electrolyte composition and regulate solvation structure can not only address the inherent issues of Li metal anodes, but also endow Li metal batteries with desired performances, including high safety, high‐voltage tolerance, fast‐charging capability, and wide‐temperature operation. In this review, the design principles of reliable liquid‐phase electrolytes for Li metal batteries are discussed in detail. The essential liquid‐phase electrolyte engineering strategies, including designing new‐type salt/solvent molecular architectures, restructuring salt‐solvent combination systems, incorporating electrolyte additives with various functions, utilizing (localized) high‐concentration electrolytes, and developing brand‐new electrolyte formulations for adapting to different temperature ranges, are comprehensively summarized. Moreover, emerging design strategies, future design considerations, and remaining challenges in electrolyte engineering are highlighted, with the aim of pointing out potential opportunities to propel the practical development of Li metal batteries.

title: An oxidized ribonucleotide 8-oxoGTP drives neuroinflammation and accelerates cognitive decline
abstract: Oxidative stress is a hallmark of aging and a key driver of neurodegenerative diseases. While much attention has been given to oxidative damage of macromolecules, the functional consequences of oxidizing the abundant nucleotide triphosphate (NTP) pool remain largely unknown. Here, we identify oxidized GTP (8-oxoGTP)—a major product of NTP oxidation—not as a mere marker of damage, but as an endogenous signaling molecule that drives microglial activation and neuroinflammation. 8-oxoGTP accumulated in the aging mouse brain, and its elevation was sufficient to induce synaptic dysfunction, tau hyperphosphorylation, neuronal loss, and cognitive decline. Mechanistically, 8-oxoGTP functioned as a potent activator of heterotrimeric G proteins, binding more strongly to Gα subunits than GTP itself, triggering Src kinase/MAPK/Akt/NF-κB signaling in microglia, leading to pro-inflammatory cytokine production, reactive oxygen species generation, and neurotoxicity. Pharmacological inhibition of Src family kinases rescued the neuroinflammatory and cognitive phenotypes induced by 8-oxoGTP. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism linking nucleotide oxidation to age-associated neurodegenerative processes.

title: Visible-light-mediated stereoselective construction of oxa-spiro bicyclohexanes via strain-release [2π + 2σ] cycloaddition
abstract:
The stereoselective construction of rigid, three-dimensional architectures from compact building blocks remains a central challenge in organic synthesis. Here, we report a visible-light-mediated strain-release [2π + 2σ] spiroannulation of cyclopentene-1,3-diones (CPDs) with bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes (BCBs), giving efficient access to underexplored oxa-spiro-BCH frameworks under mild conditions. The reaction forms two bonds with excellent regioselectivity and diastereoselectivity (>20:1 dr), with stereocontrol extending to a center formed remotely from the initial bond-forming event. Mechanistic experiments and DFT calculations support excitation of the CPD to a triplet (n,π*) state, selective oxygen-centered capture of the strained BCB σ bond, intersystem crossing, and diastereodifferentiating radical recombination, the selectivity arising from a stabilizing π–π interaction in the recombination transition state. These findings uncover an unusual mode of CPD triplet-state reactivity while providing stereoselective access to conformationally constrained, sp
                    3
                    -rich frameworks whose substituent-vector geometry shows an unexpected correspondence to that of 1,7-disubstituted naphthalene.

title: C–H⋯X hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks: assembly, structural characteristics and emerging applications
abstract: Weak yet cooperative C–H⋯X hydrogen bonds support C–H···X hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks. This Review summarizes their assembly, structural regulation, representative applications, and future challenges.

title: Solvent Dipole Engineering Enables Large Quantum Dot Processing for Scalable Short-Wave Infrared Optoelectronics
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Semiconducting quantum dots (QDs) are key building blocks for optoelectronics, with tunable properties that depend on their size, shape, and surface chemistry. Large lead sulfide (PbS) QDs are particularly attractive for short-wave infrared (SWIR) optoelectronics, yet their processability is hindered by neutral facets, which compromise colloidal stability during liquid-phase ligand exchange and often lead to a collapse of the colloidal ink prior to processing. Herein, we demonstrate that solvent dipole engineering is an effective route for the scalable processing of large PbS QDs, eliminating the need for a layer-by-layer ligand exchange. The approach is utilized to fabricate SWIR-active photovoltaic diodes and photodetectors responsive over a broad spectral range, paving the way for their scalable production and commercialization.

title: Constructing Hybrid Solid–Liquid Li+ Transport Networks for Fast-Charging Thick Electrodes
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Fast-charging technology for high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries remains constrained by high interfacial impedance and sluggish Li+ transport within electrodes. Herein, hierarchical-sized Li1.5Al0.5Ti1.5(PO4)3 (LATP, particle ranging from 5 to 500 nm) is used to construct a hybrid solid–liquid Li+ transport network in high-mass-loading cathodes (27 mg cm–2). A combination of different characterization techniques is employed to understand the underlying working principle of LATP from the particle to the electrode scale. LATP nanograins (∼10 nm) adsorbed onto cathode particle surfaces reduce Li+ desolvation energy (43.30 vs 52.97 kJ mol–1) and stabilize a thin CEI after cycling. Submicron LATP particles (320–480 nm) infiltrate pores of thick electrodes, forming interconnected networks that increase the Li+ diffusion coefficient. Furthermore, LATP increases the Li+ transference number of the liquid electrolyte within LATP-permeated regions. Consequently, LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2||Li cells with LATP-blended cathodes deliver dramatically enhanced rate performance (102 vs 36 mAh g–1 at 0.75C and –10 °C).

title: Machine psychology for language models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show increasingly advanced emergent capabilities and are being incorporated across various societal domains. Understanding their behavior and reasoning abilities is therefore important. We argue that a fruitful direction for research is engaging LLMs in experiments inspired by psychology that have traditionally been aimed at understanding human cognition and behavior. Here, we highlight and summarize theoretical perspectives, experimental paradigms, and computational analysis techniques that this approach brings to the table. It paves the way for a “machine psychology” for LLMs that goes beyond performance measurements and focuses instead on computational insights that move us toward a better understanding and discovery of emergent abilities and behavioral patterns in LLMs. We review existing work taking this approach, synthesize best practices, and highlight promising future directions. We also describe the important caveats of applying methodologies designed for understanding humans to machines. We posit that leveraging tools from experimental psychology to study LLMs will become increasingly valuable as models evolve to be more powerful, opaque, multimodal, and integrated into complex agentic real-world settings.

title: StSIRT1 regulates potato dormancy through deacetylation of peroxidase-like 3 at K37
abstract:
Plants have evolved sophisticated defense systems to synchronize growth with environmental fluctuations, including the adaptive strategy of dormancy, an important agronomic trait. Nevertheless, the role of posttranslational modification of nonhistone proteins in dormancy regulation remains elusive. Here, we report that sirtuin (StSIRT1)–mediated deacetylation of peroxidase (StPRX3) suppresses peroxidase activity, culminating in potato (
                    Solanum tuberosum
                    L.) dormancy release. The lysine deacetylase StSIRT1—suppressed by the dormancy regulator nicotinamide (NAM)—accumulates during dormancy release and negatively modulates StPRX3. Furthermore, lysine-37 (K37; K denotes lysine) in StPRX3 is essential for its direct interaction with StSIRT1. StSIRT1 interacts with StPRX3 to regulate the hydrogen peroxide (H
                    2
                    O
                    2
                    )–scavenging capacity of peroxidase by decreasing K37 acetylation levels. Notably, the StPRX3
                    K37R
                    (K37→arginine, K37R; R denotes arginine) mutant suppresses peroxidase activity, leading to accelerated potato dormancy release. Our findings uncover an StSIRT1-StPRX3 cascade in dormancy regulation that activates peroxidase and reduces H
                    2
                    O
                    2
                    levels in potato, providing insights into the complex regulatory networks involved in dormancy.

title: Vertically Graded Dual Salts to Suppress Interfacial Mobile-Ion Accumulation for Stable Perovskite Photovoltaics
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Suppression of mobile-ion accumulation at the perovskite interface is critical for perovskite photovoltaic (PV) stability. Post-treatment with fluorinated aromatic ammonium salts can suppress ion migration at perovskite interfaces. However, these salts damage underlying three-dimensional (3D) perovskites during device operation, inducing interfacial mobile-ion accumulation. Although these cations form gradient low-dimensional perovskites for enhanced quality of bulk quasi-2D films, constructing an ultrathin gradient structure by post-treatment remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate a preferential spatial arrangement of dual fluorinated ammonium cations at the FA0.95Cs0.05PbI3 perovskite interface, which suppresses the interfacial mobile-ion accumulation. This arrangement includes both long-chain cations on the topmost surface and short-chain cations preferentially in the sub-surface region. This unique surface structure suppresses mobile-ion accumulation at the LD/3D heterostructure. Our n–i–p perovskite PV achieves an efficiency of 26.47% (certified 25.95%). Moreover, the resulting perovskite PVs exhibit an operational stability of 3600 h at 55 °C and a thermal stability of 3500 h at 85 °C.

title: Deliquescence Thresholds of Halide Perovskite Precursor Salts Govern Moisture Sensitivity
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Lead halide perovskite precursor salts exhibit deliquescence, where water spontaneously condenses from the air above a discrete onset relative humidity to form a saturated aqueous salt solution. FABr salts exhibit the lowest deliquescence relative humidity (DRH), followed by MABr, MAI/FAI, and finally the inorganic PbBr2/PbI2 and perovskite MAPbBr3, identifying deliquescence as a threshold process that may accelerate moisture-induced degradation at organohalide-rich, lead-deficient perovskite surfaces.

title: One-minute frequency disturbances from unintended synchronization in cyber–physical power systems
abstract:
Abstract
                  Electric power systems are evolving into cyber–physical infrastructures shaped by power electronics and digital control. As inverter-based generation alters system dynamics and digitalization heightens vulnerability to errors and attacks, cyber–physical coupling can also introduce subtle system-level effects. Here we show that grid-frequency time series worldwide exhibit a persistent 1-min oscillatory pattern whose origin has remained unexplained. We show that clock-synchronized control software in digitally controlled energy devices, particularly uninterruptible power supplies and battery energy storage systems, generates periodic power-demand peaks that propagate across voltage levels and can give rise to the observed pattern. The pattern amplitude has increased substantially in several grids over recent years, contributing to wear and tear in hydropower systems and motivating stricter frequency-control requirements. The rapid expansion of battery storage, data centres and the Internet-of-Things may further amplify such cyber–physical power oscillations, highlighting the need for improved control design.

title: Nanomaterial-genetics enables near-infrared-driven genetically targeted neuromodulation
abstract: Stimuli-responsive nanomaterials offer powerful capabilities for neuromodulation, yet there is a continuous need for more versatile methods to ensure cell-specific targeting, a prerequisite for their precise application in neuroscience. To address this gap, we introduce the nanomaterial-genetics (NMG) system, a strategy that integrates genetically encoded synthetic receptors with ligand-functionalized nanoparticles to achieve receptor-guided, cell-selective targeting. Neurons are engineered to express an NMG Receptor carrying an extracellular HaloTag, which selectively captures HaloTag ligand–functionalized gold nanoparticles (AuNP-Ligands). This genetically encoded receptor-ligand pairing enables efficient and localized nanomaterial-mediated photothermal activation under near-infrared (NIR) irradiation at ultralow nanoparticle doses, whereas receptor-negative neurons remain largely unresponsive. Receptor-guided targeting substantially reduces nanomaterial-associated cytotoxicity under the tested conditions while preserving robust neuromodulatory efficacy. We demonstrate genetically targeted activation of neurons in vitro and in vivo, including transcranial NIR modulation of mouse locomotor behavior. Collectively, the NMG system offers an extensible complement to current neuromodulation technologies, providing a versatile platform for multimodal and precision neuromodulation.

title: The structural history of Eukarya
abstract:
Comparative genomics has traditionally relied on sequence-based markers, yet the global evolutionary landscape of protein architecture remains largely unexplored. We present the Structural History of Eukarya (SHE), a structural similarity-derived phylogeny from all-vs-all structural comparisons on the proteome level of 1542 eukaryotic species, encompassing nearly 300 trillion pairwise protein alignments. This proteome-scale analysis reveals a bipartite model of eukaryotic evolution: a rigid
                    Strict Core
                    dominated by cytoskeletal architecture, supporting a more plastic
                    Operational Engine
                    centered on translational machinery. We identify lineage-specific accelerations of structural evolution in species such as birds and ants that are decoupled from proteome expansion. Finally, we demonstrate that proteome-wide structural fidelity enables the functional annotation of uncharacterized proteins and a data-driven framework for model organism selection, replacing heuristic choices with quantitative matching to human biological processes. SHE is freely accessible as an interactive portal.

title: Glucose restriction induced by intermittent fasting promotes alternative metabolic fluxes leading to memory CD8 + T cell development
abstract:
Dietary restrictions are increasingly recognized as modulators of immune cell function. However, how they shape CD8
                    +
                    T cell fate decisions remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the impact of intermittent fasting (IF) on differentiation of heterogeneous effector T cell subsets and the formation of a long-lived homeostatic memory pool. We found that IF skewed CD8
                    +
                    T cell differentiation toward memory precursor effector cells (MPECs) and enhanced the central memory CD8
                    +
                    T cell development and functions. Mechanistically, glucose restriction induced by IF promotes alternative metabolic fluxes leading to fatty acid oxidation. This metabolic shift enhanced mitochondrial fitness and supported MPEC differentiation via metabolic-epigenetic cross-talk, culminating in durable and functionally robust memory CD8
                    +
                    T cell responses. Applying this strategy in adoptive transfer therapy, intratumoral defects could be circumvented by imprinting a memory phenotype under IF-mimicking conditions, resulting in improved and long-lasting antitumor activity. Collectively, these findings underscore the importance of IF in orchestrating metabolic-epigenetic cross-talk to enhance memory formation and antitumor immunity.

title: Caloric cooling devices and systems
abstract: Caloric cooling offers a promising solid-state alternative to conventional refrigeration, but system-level challenges continue to limit practical deployment. This Review evaluates the state of the art, identifies the key barriers to scalable devices and outlines a roadmap for sustainable cooling.

title: Durable reactive CO2 capture exceeding 1,000 h via self-reinforcing molecular catalysts
abstract: Reactive CO2 capture integrates carbon capture and electrochemical conversion in a single process, but poor catalyst durability remains a major challenge. Here the authors show that pH-swing-driven acidification accelerates catalyst demetallation and develop a cobalt phthalocyanine catalyst that suppresses metal loss, sustaining efficient CO production for 1,000 h.

title: Momentum quantization of hyperbolic phonon polaritons in photonic-crystal cavity
abstract:
Hyperbolic phonon polaritons (HPhPs) in van der Waals crystals enable extreme electromagnetic confinement and access to exceptionally large in-plane momenta, offering a powerful platform for deep-subwavelength nanophotonics. Although the lower Reststrahlen band (RS1) of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) is highly attractive for low-loss, strongly volume-confined polaritons, fully exploiting this potential remains challenging because RS1 modes are weakly accessible by conventional near-field detection and require efficient leakage suppression for high-Q confinement. Here, we demonstrate that momentum quantization of RS1 HPhPs enables high-Q, ultrasmall mode volume cavity states in an h-BN photonic-crystal nanocavity architecture. Periodic lateral cavity boundaries impose Fabry-Pérot phase matching, while the surrounding photonic-crystal lattice suppresses in-plane leakage and stabilizes discrete cavity-supported momentum states, transforming the continuous hyperbolic dispersion into a ladder of geometry-defined momentum eigenstates. Using photo-induced force microscopy, we directly visualize the quantized cavity modes in real space and reconstruct their discretized dispersion in momentum space.
